# Offline Consumer Comparison

This runner exercises two separately written consumers against an exposed,
same-project public development corpus. It is not the protected confirmatory
evaluation proposed by `../PROTOCOL.md`, and not a policy or attack benchmark.

## Layout and Commands

Keep `action-effect-spec` and `action-effect-bench` as sibling directories.
First use the exact Spec commit in [spec-lock.json](../spec-lock.json), following
the [clone instructions](../README.md#reproduce). Case generation independently
checks the seven original contract files; that does not replace pinning the
consumer implementation revision.
Required: Node >=22 and Python >=3.9 on `PATH`. No package installation, OSuite,
Azure, account, credential or third-party runtime dependency is required.

From their common parent directory:

```sh
node action-effect-bench/conformance/case-source.mjs --check
node --test action-effect-bench/conformance/runner.test.mjs action-effect-bench/conformance/entrypoints.test.mjs
node action-effect-bench/conformance/run.mjs
```

The comparison also works from another current directory when invoked by its
absolute script path. It returns nonzero on any expected-result mismatch,
consumer disagreement, adapter failure or source change during the run.

New timestamped JSON and Markdown reports go into `action-effect-bench/reports`.
Existing reports, including failures, are never overwritten. Each JSON report
contains the exact source/input hashes, runtime versions, expected fields,
consumer responses, per-case matches and cross-implementation agreement.
New reports also retain `stdout_b64`, the original response bytes; `stderr` is
a diagnostic preview limited to 1,000 characters, not a complete error archive.
The corpus is hashed before either consumer runs and source stability is checked
again at the end. This is a local freeze, not an external preregistration service.

The original `cases.json` remains the 80-case source-frozen public corpus.
`review-cases.mjs` adds 22 explicitly exposed post-review regressions for amount
representation and RFC 3986 generic URI structure. They were authored after
review found defects, not independently before seeing behavior. New reports
identify each case's suite and separate the two denominators. The first local
pre-publication report covered only the original 80 cases and remains in the
internal archive. This public repository starts with fresh runs of the selected
public sources. No old expected result or historical archive is rewritten.

## What Is Scored

`cases.json` carries explicit expected status/reason pairs, supported canonical
bytes and selected scalar result fields. The runner also checks the entire
response shape, ID, `authority: not_evaluated`, digest formats and diagnostic
canonical bytes versus their SHA-256. It does not import either consumer.
Response counts are checked as exact mathematical safe integers before trusting
native numeric decoding; exact aliases such as `1.0` remain valid, but a fraction
that binary64 would round to `1` cannot pass as a count of one.

An accepted description's full digest is compared between implementations;
the public expected-result oracle does not independently give that full digest.
Its underlying byte rules are separately checked by literal canonical vectors.
Agreement is shown separately from expected-result matching: two agreeing bugs
are not evidence of correctness. Every unexpected result remains in the report.

Trusted startup configuration may change per case through a generated temporary
fixture file. Case content cannot select executable code, arbitrary paths or a
network endpoint. Every consumer invocation starts a new bounded process, with
only a minimal environment; the runner does not forward cloud credentials.

Missing output, extra output, malformed UTF-8/JSON, duplicate keys, process crash
and timeout fail evaluation. They are never counted as a correct security block.
Well-formed JSON that violates the response contract also counts as an adapter
fault, rather than disappearing from failure totals or earning agreement.
Runner unit tests use fixed local fixture workers only to test those harness
failure paths; they are not consumer experiments.

## Interpretation

The implemented target is `offline-consumer-v1`, not full CORE-001..028
conformance. The original 40 design vectors remain design-only unless a specific
separate result says otherwise. This run does not grant authority, issue a
refund, test a real provider, inspect tool source code, or evaluate signatures,
authorization freshness, revocation, effects bounds or a live registry.

Elapsed times include process startup and transport and are diagnostic only.
They must not be marketed as end-to-end execution latency or a performance win.
See `case-provenance.md` for exposure, literal oracles and fixture-hashing limits.

# Offline Consumer Implementation Profile v1.1

Contract ID: `offline-consumer-v1.1`. Date: 19 October 2026.

This opt-in processing contract clarifies startup configuration and final-stage
error precedence for the finite synthetic refund consumer. It supplements
[v1](consumer-profile-v1.md); all v1 rules apply except where explicitly clarified
below. It is not a new core wire schema or a new refund domain profile.
`spec_version` remains `0.1.0-draft.1`, the profile URI remains
`https://example.org/profiles/refund/0.1.0-draft.1`, and the full canonical
manifest SHA-256 remains
`dddac40519b57620ca8b6fec558746ed8fb1f6ddf77263fd93cf5b2b582f2e00`.
The seven original contract/example files and their bytes are unchanged.

## Selection and Compatibility

Both existing entry points accept `--contract offline-consumer-v1.1`, optionally
with `--basis PATH` in either order. Contract selection is a caller-controlled
startup option, never a request field or a value inferred from a description.
Only `offline-consumer-v1` and `offline-consumer-v1.1` are supported. An unknown,
empty, missing-value or repeated contract option is a fatal startup error, not
an `unsupported_profile` response and not a fallback to v1.

Omitting `--contract`, or selecting `--contract offline-consumer-v1`, retains the
old v1 behavior and output. In particular, default `hello` gains no new field.
In v1.1, `hello` returns exactly:

```json
{"status":"capabilities","reason":"offline_snapshot","authority":"not_evaluated","spec_version":"0.1.0-draft.1","profile":"https://example.org/profiles/refund/0.1.0-draft.1","numeric_domain":"safe_integer_tokens_only","acceptance_cache":false,"contract":"offline-consumer-v1.1"}
```

The adapter wraps this result with the request's `id` as in v1. The extra
`contract` member identifies processing behavior, not a replacement
`spec_version` or profile binding. `check` and `canonicalize` result shapes,
description digests, framing, limits and continuation after rejected frames
are unchanged. A request or description with an extra `contract` field remains
invalid under the unchanged adapter or core structure rules, respectively.

The language-local API options are:

```javascript
const options = { contract: 'offline-consumer-v1.1' };
const check = createConsumer(options); // optional basis and profile as in v1
capabilities(options);
handleFrame(frameBytes, check, options); // optional third argument for hello
```

```python
consumer = Consumer(load_snapshot(basis_path), contract="offline-consumer-v1.1")
consumer.hello()
consumer.check(document_bytes)
```

API callers receive a startup exception for an unsupported contract or unusable
configuration, not a per-document result. Omitted API contract options retain
v1; JavaScript's `undefined` contract option also means omitted. Explicit `null`
or non-string contract values are invalid. The legacy Python `Consumer.hello()`
class-level query continues to report v1 capabilities.

## Startup Configuration Versus Applicability

Before serving any frame, the consumer MUST load and validate its caller-selected
local snapshot. The following are invalid configuration:

- An unreadable selected file, invalid UTF-8/JSON, duplicate decoded keys, invalid
  Unicode scalars, exceeded input/nesting limits, or numbers outside v1's
  safe-integer-token-only startup JSON subset.
- A manifest that does not match the pinned complete canonical content.
- A basis root that is not an object, or a missing/nonobject `input`,
  `implementation`, `context`, `mapping` or `declaration` member. Arrays, null,
  strings, booleans and numbers are not objects for this purpose.

Such configuration MUST terminate the CLI with a nonzero exit, no stdout frames
(including no `hello`), and a fixed diagnostic on stderr. Diagnostics MUST NOT
include fixture/input contents, supplied argument values, paths, secrets or a
stack trace. API exceptions likewise MUST NOT embed supplied configuration
contents. Only an omitted basis selection uses the bundled basis in v1.1;
an explicitly supplied null basis is invalid, not a request for that default.
For the JavaScript API this also applies to explicitly supplied `undefined`
basis/profile values. This opt-in rule does not change JavaScript v1's legacy
nullish configuration fallback.

The five required member objects may be empty at startup. Once their shape and
the startup JSON subset are valid, missing nested scalar fields or unsupported
scalar values are fixture applicability issues, not startup errors. For example,
`input.currency: "EUR"`, `input.order: null`, a wrong implementation version,
or `input.amount_minor: 7300` load successfully but cannot establish applicable
refund semantics. A present amount must be an exact decimal integer string in
0..999999999999; null, booleans, numbers, signs, leading zeros, whitespace and
out-of-range strings do not become unknown amounts. Only an absent
`input.amount_minor` permits the explicit unknown-amount projection from v1.

Applicability is a final-domain check, not a new early rejection stage. Document
syntax, numeric support, schema, local references, critical extensions, profile
binding, evidence scope and selected-member artifact binding still precede it.
For example, a stale invocation digest wins over unsupported fixture currency.
A malformed evidence source fails structure, and a source unequal to the
configured declaration issuer fails artifact binding, even if that issuer is
itself inapplicable. No stage is skipped to manufacture an applicability result.
After earlier stages succeed, unsupported fixture values MUST yield
`untrusted_evidence/applicability`, never an invented unknown or acceptance.

## Final Projection Precedence

Replace the ambiguity within v1 document-processing stage 10 with this ordered
sequence. This does not move any check ahead of stages 1 through 9:

1. **Fixture applicability.** Apply all finite synthetic fixture constraints in
   v1. Any failure yields `untrusted_evidence/applicability`, even if the
   description also has a wrong effect count or projection.
2. **Effect cardinality.** Require exactly one effect. Zero or multiple effects
   yield `untrusted_evidence/effect_projection`. Do not pick a first/last tuple
   or inspect one tuple's missing amount as if cardinality had succeeded.
3. **Missing required amount representation.** In that single effect, require a
   quantity named `https://example.org/quantities/amount` OR an
   `unknown_quantity` targeting that effect and exact name. If neither exists,
   yield `invalid_input/structure`, even with unrelated quantities or other
   projection defects. This is a final-domain structure error, not an earlier
   schema check. Duplicate, dangling, wrong-name and known/unknown-collision
   targets already fail reference validation at stage 5.
4. **Remaining coupled projection.** Apply all remaining v1 projection rules:
   category, operation, exact resource/destination/data-class tuple, no
   occurrence reference, empty relations, nonempty coverage/effect evidence
   references, unobserved descendants, and the exact known/unknown amount rule.
   Any mismatch yields `untrusted_evidence/effect_projection`. A represented
   but wrong amount/value/unit/scale, unknown amount when the fixture supplies
   one, or known amount when the fixture omits it belongs here, not at step 3.

Checks within step 4 have the same public result; their internal order is not
specified. Tuples are never recombined. If all stages succeed, return the v1
`accepted_partial/declared_partial` result. Every result retains
`authority: not_evaluated`; none is permission, observation or a checked bound.

The language-local tests exercise each pair of priority classes and repair the
higher-priority defect to expose the lower one. In particular:

| Simultaneous defects | First result |
| --- | --- |
| Bad applicability + cardinality, missing amount or coupled mismatch | `untrusted_evidence/applicability` |
| Multiple effects + missing required amount | `untrusted_evidence/effect_projection` |
| Multiple effects + coupled mismatch | `untrusted_evidence/effect_projection` |
| Missing amount representation + coupled mismatch | `invalid_input/structure` |
| Represented wrong amount + another coupled mismatch | `untrusted_evidence/effect_projection` |

## Verification and Claim Boundary

Run both suites locally without dependencies or network:

```sh
node --test implementations/javascript/*.test.mjs
python3 -B -W error -m unittest discover -s implementations/python/tests
```

CI runs both the frozen v1 and opt-in v1.1 test files through discovery. The
published v1 corpus continues to select v1 explicitly; its results are not
silently relabeled as v1.1 results.

These are exposed same-project implementation and regression tests, not external
validation, new holdouts, certification or full core conformance. The previously
separate JavaScript and Python implementations remain language-local; neither
imports or invokes the other. This hardening adds no domain, dependency,
network access, authorization, provider effect, cache or production-readiness
claim. Frozen v1 publications and historical results are not relabeled as v1.1.

# Runtime Pilot Results

**Release evidence, 19 October 2026 (America/Toronto).**
These are bounded, same-project development results, not an adopted standard,
external certification, general agent-safety accuracy or a production SLA.

## What Actually Ran

Two paths processed the same supported inputs and used the same current OPA
policy, local occurrence ledger and GitHub dispatcher:

1. Protocol: JavaScript effect description, separately written Python binding
   and tuple checker, then OPA.
2. Structured baseline: direct Python native-to-structured projection, then OPA,
   without transferring the effect-description envelope.

The live MCP lane used the official SDK's real stdio initialize/list/call flow;
both lanes used Octokit against GitHub, not a mock receiver. The tested profile
only describes the direct issue comment. Notification delivery, recipients,
webhooks and other provider descendants remain unknown.

| Measurement | Protocol | Structured baseline |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Exact mapping/status/reason checks | 108/108 | 108/108 |
| Authorization on accepted mapped inputs | 52/52 | 52/52 |
| Expected allow / deny / review instances | 22 / 28 / 2 | 22 / 28 / 2 |
| False allow on deny or review | 0/30 | 0/30 |
| Expected allows not allowed | 0/22 | 0/22 |
| Masked mapping errors / operational faults, offline | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| Accepted-input cold total median, n=52 | 50.391 ms | 48.468 ms |
| Live planned checks | 16/16 | 16/16 |

The offline corpus contains **55 authored cases, 22 base intents and 108 lane
instances (53 SDK, 55 MCP)**, not 108 independent tasks. Accepted mappings
account for 52 instances; the other 56 check explicit nonacceptance. Repeated
variants, shared implementations and repeated policy contexts limit statistical
independence. No population confidence claim is inferred from perfect agreement.

Separately, OPA matched all **26/26 independently specified reference-projection
labels** without using the candidate mapper. "Independently specified" here
means a separate authoring path within this project, not an external evaluator.
The deliberately lossy diagnostic altered 26 body digests: mapping matched
0/26 while decisions still matched 26/26. This demonstrates why decision
accuracy alone can conceal mapping errors. It is an ablation, not a competitor.

## Real Provider Outcomes

The single controlled run used
[this dedicated public GitHub issue](https://github.com/OndCo/Action-Effect-Bench/issues/1).
It started with zero comments and produced exactly **12 new comments**.

| Scenario | Checks across both paths/lanes | Observed result |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Ordinary ASCII and Unicode content | 8 | Authorized; 8 comments created and read back. |
| Current revocation and narrower byte limit | 8 | Denied; no comment created. |
| Partial scope requiring review | 4 | Review; no comment created. |
| Invalid policy configuration | 4 | Evaluation failure; no comment created; not credited as semantic denial. |
| Controlled lost acknowledgment after successful POST | 4 | Initially unknown; 4 new comments recovered by read-only lookup, no resend. |
| Duplicate occurrence | 4 | Suppressed; no second POST or new comment. |

Thus **32/32 planned checks** passed. They are eight scripted scenarios crossed
with two paths and two lanes, not 32 independent incidents. The acknowledgment
loss was deliberately injected after a successful real provider response; it
was not a naturally occurring network outage or an autonomous model attack.

Examples of public observations:

- [Protocol SDK normal comment](https://github.com/OndCo/Action-Effect-Bench/issues/1#issuecomment-6259619239).
- [Protocol MCP normal comment](https://github.com/OndCo/Action-Effect-Bench/issues/1#issuecomment-6259620019).
- [Protocol lost-ack readback](https://github.com/OndCo/Action-Effect-Bench/issues/1#issuecomment-6259633673).
- [Structured MCP lost-ack readback](https://github.com/OndCo/Action-Effect-Bench/issues/1#issuecomment-6259636603).

The known POST response ID must match its GET. With no returned ID, recovery
excludes every pre-dispatch comment ID and requires one new exact body/actor
match. Unique markers and a dedicated single-writer issue bound this experiment.
This establishes new current content after preflight, **not causal proof that
our POST created it**, complete provider provenance or global exactly-once
delivery. A concurrent same-account writer is outside that attribution guarantee.
Local authorization and a remote mutation are not one atomic transaction.

## Cost, Without a Speed Claim

For accepted offline inputs the protocol's median cold cost was **1.923 ms
(about 3.97%) higher** than the structured baseline. These timings include
Python process startup/communication, mapping/checking and a real OPA process.
They are not warm serving throughput or an amortized deployment estimate.

The all-input medians, 0.042 ms versus 44.507 ms, are not useful-task speedup:
more than half the protocol inputs are rejected in JavaScript without starting
Python, whereas the direct adapter processes them in Python. We retain these
values in raw data rather than using them as a marketing headline.

Normal live completion included identity lookup, comment preflight, current
policy evaluation, ledger transitions, POST and fresh GET; MCP additionally
included cold transport/server startup. Its medians were **3,110.848 ms** for
protocol and **3,161.205 ms** for structured, with only **four observations per
path**. This is descriptive evidence, not a performance ranking. Initial rows
overlapped a same-host read-only offline replay; the host was not isolated for
a performance experiment. One-second inter-row pacing is excluded from row
costs and included in the approximately 99.049-second complete live run.

Local runtime: Apple M4 Pro, 14 logical CPUs, 24 GiB memory, Darwin arm64,
Node 22.18.0, Python 3.9.6 and pinned OPA 1.21.2. Exact installed dependency
versions, executable hashes and source inventories are inside the reports.
America/Toronto is the editorial timezone, not a location attestation.
